newsitem.title: GERMANY: Henkel steps up offer for Loctite.
newsitem.headline: Henkel steps up offer for Loctite.

text.p: German consumer products group Henkel KGaA said Wednesday it was increasing its offer for the 65 percent stake it does not already own in adhesives-maker Loctite Corp.

The increase to $57.75 a share, which values all of Hartford, Conn.-based Loctite at $1.2 billion, was widely expected after Henkel's announcement last week that it had made an offer to the Loctite board "in the area of $56."

In response, Loctite, which makes sealants, adhesives and lubricants, issued a brief statement Wednesday saying it was evaluating the bid and urging stockholders not to accept or reject Henkel's offer until it announced its recommendation.
Loctite's shares gained 75 cents to $58.625 in afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange, indicating that investors believed a higher bid was possible.
Analysts said last week that a final offer of $60 could not be ruled out.
Henkel's board said in a statement Wednesday that it was still seeking to hold discussions with Loctite aimed at securing a friendly takeover of the company.
In its brief statement Wednesday Loctite said merely that a special committee of its board was in the process of reviewing Henkel's offer.

Henkel said its new offer, which is open until Jan. 6, would be valid only if acceptances allow Henkel to increase its existing 35 percent stake past the 50 percent threshold that would give it control of Loctite.
Shares in Henkel closed 65 pfennigs (43 cents) higher at 69.95 German marks ($46) on the Frankfurt stock exchange after trading as high as 70.80 marks ($46.58).
German analysts applauded the deal as reinforcing Henkel's leadership in the world market for industrial and commercial adhesives.

However, chemical industry analysts also noted that Loctite's earnings growth in the past four years has not been strong and that Loctite has not appeared to benefit greatly from the growth in demand for adhesives seen this year.
There were also concerns in Germany about the impact the deal would have on Henkel's debt.

Such a deal would double Henkel's current debt levels, which contributed to the Standard & Poor's credit rating agency's decision to put the company on "CreditWatch" with negative implications last week.
Henkel has nonetheless said it planned to use debt to finance the proposed acquisition.
